title: Gas Station Loop
statement:
An electric delivery van drives a circular route past n charging stops, numbered 0 to n - 1. At stop i it can take gas[i] units of charge. Driving from stop i to the next stop (i + 1, or 0 after the last one) uses cost[i] units. The battery has no upper limit and starts empty.

Write def solution(gas, cost) that returns the index of a stop where the van can start, charge, and drive one full loop back to that stop without the charge ever going below 0. Return -1 if no start works. In the classic version the answer is guaranteed to be unique; here, if several stops work, return the smallest index.

examples.why: The LeetCode 134 example 1. Gains are -2, -2, -2, +3, +3; starting at 3 the charge goes 3, 6, 4, 2, 0.
The LeetCode 134 example 2. The route needs 10 units but only 9 are available.
A single stop: take 5, use 4 to come back to it.

think.q: What happens at each stop, in which order?
think.a: At stop i you add gas[i], then drive and subtract cost[i]. The charge after that drive must be ≥ 0. Only the difference gas[i] - cost[i] matters, so think of a list of gains and losses around a circle: you need a starting point where the running sum never dips below 0.

Gains: -2, -2, -2, +3, +3. Total 0, so a loop is possible in principle. Starting at 0 fails at once (-2). Starting at 3: 3, 6, then 4, 2, 0. Never negative, so 3. Notice that starts 0, 1 and 2 all fail in their first step, and you could see that from one pass.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Try every start: simulate up to n steps and stop at the first negative charge. Return the first start that survives the whole loop. That is O(n^2) when many starts fail late.

Greedy with two facts. First, if the total of all gains is negative, no start works. Second, if you start at s and first run dry after stop j, then no start between s and j works either: starting at such a stop k means arriving there with 0 charge instead of the ≥ 0 you had, so you run dry by j as well. So jump the candidate to j + 1 and reset the charge. One pass finds the candidate; if the total is ≥ 0 the candidate completes the loop. Every earlier stop was ruled out, so it is also the smallest valid start.

1. total = tank = start = 0.
  2. For each i: diff = gas[i] - cost[i]; add it to total and to tank.
  3. If tank < 0: set start = i + 1 and tank = 0.
  4. Return start if total ≥ 0, else -1.

One stop (works if gas ≥ cost). A total that is short by 1. Every stop with gain 0, where every start works and the answer is 0. Two valid starts, where the smallest must win. A start at the last index, which needs the wrap-around. A start found after several failures.

hints: Only gas[i] - cost[i] matters. When is a full loop impossible no matter where you start?
If you start at s and run dry right after stop j, can any start between s and j do better?
One pass: keep a running tank; when it goes negative at i, the next candidate is i + 1 with an empty tank. Also keep the grand total; if it is negative, return -1.
solution:
def solution(gas, cost):
    total = 0      # sum of all gains: negative means no start can work
    tank = 0       # charge since the current candidate start
    start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        diff = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total += diff
        tank += diff
        if tank < 0:
            # Every start from `start` to i runs dry by here: try the next stop.
            start = i + 1
            tank = 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1
explain:
Example 1, gas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], cost = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], gains [-2, -2, -2, 3, 3]:

  • i = 0: tank -2 < 0. Start 0 is out: start = 1, tank 0.
  • i = 1: tank -2: start = 2. i = 2: tank -2: start = 3.
  • i = 3: tank 3. i = 4: tank 6.
  • total = 0 ≥ 0: return 3.

Why the candidate is safe without simulating the wrap-around: the pass split the stops before 3 into failed segments (here [0], [1] and [2]). Each one stays ≥ 0 until its last stop and has a negative sum. From stop 3 the van reaches the end of the row with T = 6. Inside each failed segment the charge stays at least what it was on entry, and after its last stop it is T plus the sums of the segments so far. Each segment sum is negative, so that is smallest after the last segment, where it equals total ≥ 0. So the charge never goes below 0, and one O(n) pass is enough.

tests.why: every start works: the smallest is 0

tests.why: start 0 runs dry after stop 1; stop 2 works
